  "brief": "Solid, corrected evidence exists for Etherpad (OT) and Yjs/Automerge (CRDT) failure patterns via their own issue trackers plus OT/interleaving literature; ShareDB adds further OT evidence. Google Docs appears only via explanatory blogs (no incident/postmortem evidence), Figma is explicitly described as neither OT nor CRDT, and Notion has zero coverage in these sources — treat any claim about those three as unsupported beyond architecture description. Where evidence exists: OT failures cluster around transform/version/state-machine correctness, producing divergence, rejected ops, corruption, or crashes; CRDT failures cluster around metadata/memory/sync cost and semantic interleaving, with actual duplication/corruption traced to editor bindings or providers rather than the merge algorithm itself. Confidence is medium: the underlying draft misattributed several citations to wrong sources, which have been corrected here, and most evidence is scattered single GitHub issues rather than systematic postmortems.",
  "report": "## 1. What the evidence actually covers\n\nThe question names five product families: Google Docs, Etherpad, ShareDB-based apps, Figma, Notion, and Yjs/Automerge-based products. Coverage in the supplied sources is uneven:\n\n- **Etherpad** and **ShareDB**: covered directly and specifically, via their own GitHub issue trackers, wikis, and one operational incident report [s5][s8]. This is the strongest OT evidence in the set.\n- **Yjs** and **Automerge**: covered directly via issue trackers, reference docs, and academic papers on sequence/rich-text CRDT design [s31][s32][s33][s34][s37][s39][s41][s42][s46][s48][s50][s55][s61]. This is the strongest CRDT evidence in the set.\n- **Google Docs**: covered only by secondary explanatory/system-design blog posts [s2][s3][s6][s10][s13][s14][s122], never by a primary Google engineering incident report or postmortem. These sources support describing Google Docs' architecture as OT-style, but **none** document a specific production failure of Google Docs. A claim of an actual Google Docs corruption incident would be unsupported by this evidence.\n- **Figma**: covered by two sources that explicitly describe its multiplayer engine as neither classical positional OT nor a sequence/text CRDT, but a server-ordered flat-object-map model with its own conflict mechanics [s76][s78]. Figma cannot be used here as an OT or CRDT failure example without misrepresenting the sources.\n- **Notion**: no source in the list addresses Notion's editing engine, architecture, or incidents at all. Nothing below describes Notion; its mention in the question is unsupported by this evidence.\n\nEverything that follows is therefore an evidence-grounded account of OT failures in **Etherpad and ShareDB**, and CRDT failures in **Yjs and Automerge**, cautiously generalized to the two algorithm classes, with Google Docs and Figma noted only as architectural illustrations and Notion excluded.\n\n## 2. OT failure modes documented in the evidence\n\n| Failure mode | Root cause | Observable symptom | Evidence |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Concurrent text+attribute changes not transformed correctly; server rejects the result with a bad-changeset / \"illegal edit\" error | Implementation bug in the changeset/attribute transform path, not the OT theorem itself | Rejected edits, missing formatting, \"classified illegal\" errors, sometimes disconnection | [s19][s25][s27] |
| Pad corruption requiring manual DB repair; overwritten pads with stale revisions left behind | Persistence/state-management implementation bug, separate from transform correctness | Visible document corruption; admins must reset/sanitize DB entries; DB bloat from retained stale revisions | [s21][s28] |
| Multi-server ShareDB deployments desynchronize; clients see \"Invalid op submitted, op version newer than current snapshot\" | Deployment architecture: pub/sub messages shared across servers but document state/snapshots were not, so servers disagreed on current version | Rejected operations, halted synchronization until architecture (shared persistent store) was fixed | [s90][s89][s92] |
| Reconnect/client state-machine gaps: local edits render but are not retransmitted until another edit is made; pads silently disconnect when a browser suspends a background tab; connection timeouts too short on poor networks | Client-side reconnect/queue logic and network-timeout configuration, not the transform algorithm | Edits appear locally but are invisible to others until a further edit; silent disconnection; premature drops on weak connections | [s29][s111][s103][s105] |
| Cursor/presence synchronization is not a built-in OT primitive and had to be requested/added separately | Design gap: OT libraries model document operations, not auxiliary presence channels, so apps bolt this on themselves | Cursor/selection inconsistency as a distinct class of bug from document divergence | [s98] |
| Server-side performance failures: slow startup and changeset timeouts, configuration-driven slowdowns, database/performance questions from operators, requests to split large pad content | Server implementation, configuration and DB layer, amplified by growing changeset/revision history that OT must retain | Slow startup, timeouts, operator-visible performance complaints, feature requests to shard pad content | [s101][s102][s106][s108][s109] |
| Process-level instability: JSON-related errors shutting the server down; crashes on install or when installing plugins | Implementation/integration bugs at the server or plugin layer | Server or process crash rather than a wrong document state | [s104][s107][s110] |
| Rebasing offline/old client operations against server history becomes progressively more expensive, and history truncation can strand very stale in-flight operations | Not evidenced here as a specific production incident; this is a design-level property discussed in the classical and formal OT literature (need for order-independent transformation properties such as TP1/TP2, and correctness proofs for transformation functions) | Analytically implies CPU spikes, slow reconnects, or forced resync, but no production incident report in this source set demonstrates it directly | [s119][s121][s124][s113] |\n\nAcross these, a consistent pattern emerges: the reports split into (1) genuine transform/version-state correctness errors close to the OT machinery itself [s19][s25][s27][s90][s89][s92], and (2) surrounding implementation problems — persistence, reconnect logic, timeouts, plugins, server configuration — that produce outages or rejected edits without necessarily indicating a wrong transformation function [s21][s28][s29][s103][s104][s105][s107][s109][s110][s111].\n\n## 3. CRDT failure modes documented in the evidence\n\n| Failure mode | Root cause | Observable symptom | Evidence |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Concurrent insertions at the same logical position interleave into unreadable text; specifically reported for reverse-order insertion in Automerge's classic list algorithm | Algorithmic: a deterministic total order over element identifiers does not guarantee each user's insertion stays contiguous | All replicas converge to the identical, but semantically scrambled, text | [s50][s46][s48][s53] |
| Duplicated text between two concurrently editing users in a y-prosemirror binding | Editor-binding implementation bug (cleanup code moving content between concurrent Y.Text objects), not the CRDT merge rule | Visible duplicated characters — actual corruption, not merely an interleaving artifact | [s66] |
| Rich-text structural conflicts: overlapping bold/italic/link/block edits are hard for tree-shaped representations to merge without duplication, loss, or restructuring | Partly algorithmic (generic tree/list CRDTs don't encode rich-text semantics by default); Peritext was designed specifically to fix this by anchoring formatting spans over a flat character sequence | Formatting loss, duplicated structure, or surprising formatting outcomes in naive tree-CRDT designs | [s61][s62][s68][s58] |
| Tombstones and deletion metadata accumulate, especially with offline replicas, inflating document size and memory even when the visible content is small | Algorithmic storage trade-off: safe removal requires causal knowledge that no replica can still reference an item | Slower load/sync, growing storage/memory footprint disproportionate to visible content | [s39][s35] |
| Provider/server processes leak memory as `Y.Doc`/websocket objects and awareness timers are not cleaned up after clients disconnect | Provider/lifecycle implementation bug, not the CRDT algorithm | Server memory grows with the number of previously opened sessions/documents | [s37][s41][s42] |
| Large memory spikes during document load/save operations | Implementation/serialization overhead in materializing document and change history | Transient large memory usage, risk of out-of-memory | [s33] |
| Large sync messages block the event loop, causing other clients' sockets to time out | Synchronization/message-framing implementation treating a document update as one blocking unit | Apparent disconnections/timeouts for unrelated clients sharing a process | [s32] |
| Runtime crash while receiving a sync message (WASM \"unreachable\" error) | Implementation defect in the binding/runtime layer processing incoming updates | Crash/failure to process an incoming update, not a merge-correctness issue | [s34] |
| Coarse editor-to-CRDT diffing (e.g., calling a text-update API on large accumulated changes rather than per keystroke) merges poorly | Editor-binding/API-usage issue: large snapshot diffs lose the fine-grained causal structure the CRDT expects | Worse concurrent-merge outcomes and more expensive updates, despite the document remaining convergent | [s55] |
| CRDTs can expose concurrent conflicting values explicitly (e.g., competing map assignments) rather than silently resolving them | Algorithmic design choice — convergence via deterministic tie-break, but the API surfaces the conflict rather than hiding it | Application must handle an explicit \"multiple values\" state; a genuinely different symptom class from OT's typical silent overwrite-or-reject behavior | [s56] |\n\nThe important distinction across this table: only two rows ([s66] and the WASM crash [s34]) are true visible-corruption or crash bugs, and both are binding/runtime implementation defects, not failures of the CRDT merge law. The rest of the CRDT failure surface is either (a) a semantic/interleaving artifact that is fully convergent but ugly [s50][s46][s48][s61], or (b) a performance/memory-degradation problem tied to metadata, provider lifecycle, or serialization [s39][s37][s41][s42][s33][s32].\n\n## 4. Disagreement in the evidence\n\nThe sources do not disagree on core facts, but they disagree in **framing and categorization**, which matters for anyone drawing conclusions from only part of the evidence:\n\n- **Framing disagreement (marketing vs. operations):** the Google-Docs/CRDT-vs-OT comparison blogs [s1][s4][s69] and the survey-style pieces tend to present CRDTs as the more robust, failure-resistant choice, while the CRDT projects' own issue trackers [s32][s33][s34][s37][s39][s41][s42] show CRDT implementations have a substantial, distinct failure surface of their own (memory, sync cost, crashes). Neither side is factually wrong, but a reader who only reads the comparison blogs would not learn that CRDTs fail differently rather than not at all.\n- **Categorization disagreement:** one source explicitly argues Figma's multiplayer engine was built *without* CRDTs [s76], while general comparison pieces about collaborative editing sometimes lump systems like Figma in with CRDT or OT examples without that distinction. The evidence here supports treating Figma as neither.\n- **Even within a single project, the underlying algorithm identity is disputed:** a ShareDB issue literally asks whether the library implements the Jupiter OT algorithm [s94], indicating some uncertainty among users/maintainers about which specific OT variant is in play — relevant because different OT algorithms carry different correctness guarantees (TP1 vs. TP1+TP2) [s121][s124].\n\nWhat would settle these: a primary specification document from each project stating which algorithm variant is implemented and which correctness properties it claims, rather than inference from issue-tracker discussion.\n\n## 5. How the two failure sets differ\n\n| Dimension | OT (Etherpad/ShareDB evidence) | CRDT (Yjs/Automerge evidence) |\n|---|---|---|\n| Primary correctness hazard | Wrong transformation of concurrent ops, wrong operation version/snapshot, broken client/server state machine | Ordering of concurrent inserts not matching human intention; rich-text tree merges; provider/binding bugs |\n| Where true divergence/corruption showed up | Close to the transform/version-state machinery itself [s19][s25][s27][s90][s89][s92] | Almost never in the merge algorithm; the one clear corruption case was a binding cleanup bug [s66], plus a runtime crash bug [s34] |\n| Typical visible document failure | Rejected edits, missing formatting, corrupted pads needing manual repair, DB bloat from stale revisions [s21][s28] | Convergent-but-scrambled text (interleaving) [s50][s46][s48]; formatting anomalies in naive tree merges [s61] |\n| Typical performance failure | Server-side changeset/revision growth, slow startup, timeouts, reconnect cost [s101][s102][s106][s108][s109] | Tombstone/metadata growth, provider memory leaks, large-message blocking, load/save memory spikes [s39][s35][s37][s41][s42][s33][s32] |\n| Offline/reconnect behavior | Awkward: client must resync/rebase against server's intervening history; reconnect logic itself has documented gaps [s29][s105][s111] | More natural for merging, but offline replicas increase retained history/tombstones and sync payload size [s39][s35] |\n| Semantic/interleaving behavior | Not centrally evidenced as an OT-specific artifact in this source set | Central and well-documented artifact class, arising from the ordering rule itself, independent of any implementation bug [s50][s46][s48][s53] |\n\n## 6. What remains unsettled and what would settle it\n\n- **Google Docs**: no primary incident/postmortem evidence exists in this set. Unsettled whether Google Docs has ever experienced a divergence, corruption, or performance incident of the kinds documented for Etherpad/ShareDB. A leaked or published Google engineering postmortem, or an official transparency report, would settle this.\n- **Notion**: entirely absent from the evidence. Nothing here supports any claim about Notion's editing engine or its failure history. Direct engineering write-ups or incident reports from Notion would be needed.\n- **Figma**: settled that it is neither classic OT nor sequence-CRDT by the sources' own account [s76][s78]; unsettled whether its actual failure modes resemble either category, since no failure-mode evidence for Figma specifically was provided.\n- **Statistical weight of the evidence**: almost every OT and CRDT failure cited here is a single reported GitHub issue, not an aggregated postmortem or incident-frequency study. It is unsettled how representative any single issue is of the algorithm class versus a one-off implementation bug in that specific project. A systematic bug-tracker analysis across multiple independent OT and CRDT implementations, or a controlled comparative study running identical workloads against both architectures, would be needed to make the root-cause split (algorithmic vs. implementation) more than a case-by-case judgment.\n- **The one directly-relevant algorithmic-correctness claim not backed by a specific production incident** — that rebasing costs grow with offline duration/history length — rests on classical/formal OT literature [s119][s121][s124][s113] rather than an observed production failure in this evidence set, and should be read as a design property, not a documented incident.",
  "confidence": "medium"
